sources.title: When Goals Leak Across Relationships: How Cached Goal Representations Shape Cross-Client Decisions
sources.description:
arXiv:2610.17365v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As LLM agents take on more autonomous roles, they may interact with multiple clients and counterparties whose goals and incentives conflict. If an agent maintains shared inference state across these interactions, information associated with one relationship may influence decisions made for another. We test OLMo-3-7B-Instruct in a controlled two-client environment with 20 market scenarios, where each client is assigned an opposing objective. With shared conversational memory, the model deviates from the current client's objective in 22% of eligible decisions. We then investigate how these goals are represented in the KV cache. Linear probes show that client-goal ownership becomes highly recoverable in middle layers and is concentrated in particular attention heads. We use these results to identify where to intervene in the cache and test whether these representations affect the model's decisions. Ablating the competitor's cached goal representations at these locations shifts the model toward the current client. The effect is larger for heads identified by probing than for randomly selected heads, and larger when ablating goal tokens than matched non-goal tokens from the same client. Our results show that client-specific goal representations persist in the KV cache and can causally influence decisions made for other clients, highlighting the importance of relationship-specific state isolation in persistent LLM agents.

sources.title: Enhanced Detective: A Dual-Stage Proactive Defense Against Internal Poisoning Attacks in Financial Fraud Detection Using Federated Learning
sources.description:
arXiv:2610.17523v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: With recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), the adoption of distributed learning paradigms such as Federated Learning (FL) has emerged. In simple terms, FL enables multiple entities to collaboratively train AI models without sharing local data. The FL paradigm is particularly valuable in privacy-sensitive settings, such as financial services, because it enables institutions to collaboratively improve fraud-detection models while keeping sensitive transaction data local. However, FL schemes are prone to security vulnerabilities, where malicious clients can poison local data or model updates and degrade the global model, and hence the performance of the resulting model might be affected. Therefore, in this work, we propose Enhanced Detective, a dual-stage robust aggregation strategy that combines Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), distance-based update filtering, and FedMedian aggregation. Experiments on an imbalanced credit card dataset evaluate targeted label-flipping and weight-scaling attacks over 50 communication rounds. With 40% malicious clients, Enhanced Detective achieves an AUPRC of 0.796 and a Recall of 0.847.

sources.title: FedGraph: Defending Federated Large Language Model Fine-Tuning Against Backdoor Attacks via Graph-Based Aggregation
sources.description:
arXiv:2610.18430v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) allows multiple clients to collaboratively adapt models without sharing raw data, offering strong privacy benefits. However, this setting is highly vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which malicious clients manipulate their updates to induce targeted behaviors while maintaining normal performance on benign inputs.
  In this work, we make a key observation specific to federated LLM fine-tuning: malicious clients tend to exhibit strong consistency in their model updates, whereas benign clients produce more diverse and dispersed updates. This structural difference is not well captured by existing defense methods, which typically rely on direct anomaly detection in high-dimensional parameter space and therefore struggle in the presence of entangled LLM updates.
  Motivated by this observation, we propose FedGraph, a graph-based aggregation framework that explicitly models relationships among client updates. By representing clients as nodes in a dynamically constructed graph and extracting structural features that characterize their relative positions and interactions, FedGraph derives compact client representations that effectively separate malicious and benign behaviors. These representations are then used to identify and suppress malicious contributions during aggregation.
  Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedGraph significantly improves backdoor defense. It consistently reduces attack success rates to below 10% while achieving high detection accuracy (95.5% on average) and a low false positive rate (2.33%), substantially outperforming existing federated learning defenses.

sources.title: Federated Learning with Energy-Based Structured Probabilistic Inference
sources.description:
arXiv:2606.30161v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables multiple clients to collaboratively train machine learning models without sharing their local data. However, heterogeneity in client data and the presence of unreliable or adversarial updates make effective server aggregation challenging, motivating methods that adapt client contributions according to their reliability and relationships. In this work, we formulate server aggregation in FL as structured probabilistic inference using conditional random fields. We represent clients as nodes in a graph and define unary and pairwise energy potentials. Unary potentials capture individual client properties, while pairwise potentials encode similarities between clients. This formulation treats individual client evidence and pairwise relationships as coupled evidence in a joint inference problem, allowing client reliabilities to be inferred collectively and the resulting estimates to guide aggregation. Where most FL methods target a single challenge, FedCRF's inferred reliabilities and affinities provide one common representation for global aggregation, Byzantine robustness, clustered FL, and personalized FL. With a single set of hyperparameters, it is competitive with or outperforms specialized methods on CIFAR-10, FEMNIST, and Fed-ISIC2019 across diverse forms of client heterogeneity and unreliability.
